Natural history of Sigalionidae is poorly studied. They are found
worldwide and occur from the intertidal to depths of several
thousand metres. Pisioninae are mostly found in shallow waters,
with Pisione longipalpa described from >900m (Uschakoy, 1956)
being the only exception. All Pisioninae and some Pholoinae
(Metaxypsamma, Laubierpholoe, Imajimapholoe, Taylorpholoe) are
interstitial. Pisione garciavaldecasasi is the only known freshwa-
ter species and was described from rivers in Panama (San Martin
et al., 1998).
In general, Sigalionidae, considering their jaw morphology,
are expected to be carnivorous. However, feeding habits of
Sigalionidae are largely unknown. Most Sigalioninae burrow in
soft sediments and Sthenelanella inhabits self-constructed tubes.
This indicates that they are likely to be sit-and-wait preda-
tors (Jumars et al., 2015). In fact, Pernet (2000) described such
behaviour for Sthenelais berkeleyi, where the animals burrow into
the sediment and use antero-dorsally oriented chaetae to form
a ‘chaetal snorkel’ to maintain respiration. Pholoinae are most
probably more active hunter predators, Pleijel (1983), in the only
study on the feeding biology of Pholoinae, described Pholoe balti-
ca (as Pholoe minuta) as an active predator on Spionidae, small
crustaceans, and forams. If active predation also occurs in oth-
er Sigalionidae, this remains to be shown. Heffernan et al. (1983)
reported mean densities of about 100 per 0.1 m? of Pholoe baltica
(as Pholoe minuta) from Ireland. Gonzalez et al. (2017a) discuss
the biogeographical distribution patterns of Pisione.

Sigalionidae have a convoluted taxonomic history. Histori-
cally, the group included scale-worms bearing compound
neurochaetae, corresponding largely to today’s Sigalioninae.
Rouse and Fauchald’s (1997) cladistic analyses recovered
Sigalionidae as the sister group to other Aphroditiformia that
lacked compound neurochaetae. However, subsequent analyses
based on both morphology (Pleijel and Dahlgren, 1998; Rouse
and Pleijel, 2001) and also sequence data (Gonzalez et al., 2018a;
Norlinder et al., 2012; Struck et al., 2005b; Wiklund et al., 2005;
Zhang, Y. et al., 2018a) repeatedly revealed the paraphyly of
Sigalionidae, both with regard to Pholoinae and Pisioninae.
In the most recent phylogenetic studies of Aphroditiformia by
Zhang et al., (2018a) and Gonzalez et al. (2018a), Sigalionidae
was recovered as the sister group to a clade comprising Poly-
noidae + (Iphionidae + Acoetidae). Gonzalez et al. (2018a) also
revised the classification of Aphroditiformia and there Sigalionidae
was subdivided into Pelogeniinae, Pisioninae, Pholoinae, Sigalioni-
hae, and Sthenelanellinae. We here follow their delineation of the
group, though not all the names. This makes the first described

Sigalionidae to be Pholoe longa (Miiller, 1776) (as Aphrodita lon-
ga). The phylogenetic relationships within Sigalionidae remain
problematic and warrant further study (Gonzalez et al., 2018a).
Sthenelanellinae is monotypic for Sthenelanella, making one of
the names currently superfluous and we therefore use the latter
only, The type species Sthenelanella uniformis was first named
by Moore (1910) and later the genus was revised by Pettibone
(1969b). Currently, there are only six recognized species of
Sthenelanella (Read and Fauchald, 2021). Pettibone (1997)
erected Pelogeniinae for Pelogenia, Psammolyce, Neopsammolyce,
Hartmanipsammolyce,  Dayipsammolyce,  Claparedepelogenia,
Pottsipelogenia, and Heteropelogenia, and these are the genera
considered valid today (Gonzalez et al., 2018a). Pisioninae
include the taxa Anoplopisione, Pisione, Pisionella, and Pisionidens
(Gonzalez et al., 2017b). The most species-rich group within
Pisioninae is Pisione with 46 species out of a total of 54 (Read
and Fauchald, 2021). Generic diagnoses for all Sigalionidae (excl.
Pisioninae) are provided in Eibye-Jacobsen et al. (2018) and
separately for Pisioninae in Gonzalez et al. (2017b).
Both Pholoinae and Sigalioninae also have complicated tax-
onomic histories. The former taxon currently includes Ima-
jimapholoé, Laubierpholoe, Metaxypsamma, Pholoe, and Taylor-
pholoe. Pholoinae were in earlier literature either treated as a
subgroup within Sigalionidae (e.g. Chamberlin, 1919; Levin-
sen, 1883), or as a separate group (see review in Pettibone,
1992). The family names Pholoididae and Peisidicidae were intro-
duced by Fauchald (1977) and Darboux (1900), respectively, but
synonymized with Pholoidae by Pettibone (1992). Sigalioninae
correspond largely to what was referred to as Sigalionidae in ear-
lier literature. Sigalioninae encompasses 14 genera, and now also
include Pholoides (Gonzalez et al., 2018a). Read and Fauchald
(2021) accept 249 species in Sigalionidae sensu Gonzalez et al.
(2018a).
Important early studies include Ehlers (1864) and Darboux
(1899). Major taxonomic studies include a series of revisions by
Pettibone (1969b; Pettibone 1970a; b; c; Pettibone 1971a; b), and
Mackie and Chambers (1990). Regional studies on Sigalionidae
are provided by Lana (1991b) for Brazil, Blake (1995b) for Cal-
ifornia, Wehe (2007) from around the Arabian Peninsula, and
Chambers (1985), Hartmann-Schréder (1996), Chambers and
Muir (1997) for northern Europe. Sigalion recorded from north-
ern Europe were reviewed by Muir (1989). An annotated check-
list of Sigalionidae and Pholoidae was published by Aungtonya
and Eibye-Jacobsen (2014). Most recent taxonomic additions to
the group include Martinez et al., (2008) and Petersen et al.,
(2016) for Pisioninae, Aungtonya (2007), Padovani and Amar-
al (2014), Alalykina (2018), and Aungtonya and Eibye-Jacobsen
(2018) for Sigalioninae. Barnich and Van Haaren (2021) have
published a detailed revision of Northeast Atlantic and Mediter-
ranean Sigalioninae and provide an updated identification key.
Meissner et al., (2017) used an integrative taxonomic approach
to address the diversity of Arctic Pholoe spp., including redescrip-
tions of Pholoe longa and Pholoe minuta. Dryptoscolex matthiesae
is a Carboniferous-aged fossil described by Thompson (1979).
Fitzhugh et al. (1997) considered it as part of Sigalionidae owing
to Thompson's (1979) suggestion that compound chaetae were
present.
